title: Ложные схватки и важный гость  (False Contractions and an Important Guest)

segments.t: In the dining room, Vika meets with influential official Nikolai Maryanovich to arrange a last-minute birthday banquet. Max interrupts them, furious that Vika did not tell him her contractions were false.
Я хочу закрыть ресторан на спецобслуживание.
А почему ты не в роддоме?
Now let's go back through their conversation line by line and unpack the Russian phrasing.
Я хочу закрыть ресторан на спецобслуживание.

'I want to close the restaurant for a private event.' The guest projects a direct stance straight away, linking "khochu" ("want"), "zakryt" ("to close, to shut"), and "restoran" ("restaurant") in one brisk exchange.
'I will be celebrating my birthday.' The guest establishes a firm posture straight away, joining "den" ("day") to "rozhdeniya" ("of birth") so every word pulls its weight.
'Of course, and when exactly?' Vika wonders frankly as they speak, combining "konechno" ("of course") and "kogda" ("when") so the key meaning lands right away.
'Well, tonight or tomorrow evening.' The guest strikes a thoughtful manner for Vika, building the phrase around "segodnya" ("today") and "zavtra" ("tomorrow") for a crisp, natural delivery.
'Renting the restaurant is arranged in advance.' Vika favors a direct bearing during the exchange, leaning on "arenda" ("rental") before closing the thought with "restorana" ("restaurant").
'Vika, can I have a word with you?' Max quizzes evenly without hesitation, joining "mozhno" ("may, can") to "minutu" ("a minute") so every word pulls its weight.
'Wait, I am talking right now.' Vika holds an easygoing course on the spot, putting "podozhdi" ("wait") alongside "seychas" ("now") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
А почему ты не в роддоме?
'And why are you not at the maternity hospital?' Max challenges quietly in their exchange, placing "pochemu" ("why") straight beside "roddome" ("maternity hospital") with no word for "to be" needed.
'The morning contractions turned out to be false.' Vika keeps a clear style at this moment, joining "utrenniye" ("morning") to "skhvatki" ("contractions") so every word pulls its weight.
'The doctors let me go home.' Vika presents a resolute rhythm on the spot, combining "vrachi" ("doctors") and "domoy" ("home") so the key meaning lands right away.
'Could you not have called me?' Max presses dryly across the room, putting "pozvonit" ("to call") alongside "nelzya" ("not allowed") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
'Young man, wait until we finish.' The guest conveys a calm style straight away, leaning on "yunosha" ("young man") before closing the thought with "podozhdite" ("wait").
'I will just talk to my wife!' Max presents a pointed view in front of the guest, putting "prosto" ("just") alongside "pogovoryu" ("I'll talk") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
Я хочу закрыть ресторан на спецобслуживание.
А почему ты не в роддоме?
Right after Max snaps at the VIP guest, Vika's real contractions start on the dining room floor. See you next time!
